Best you get to know how I like to work.

- Keep things simple - Channel "YAGNI" energy when coding unless otherwise instructed.
- Type safety is important, and we want to take advantage of it.
- I like when my colleagues propose bold solutions when the problem warrants it.
- I like doing documentation first development (see below)
- Avoid one line functions that are just wrappers

- `any` is the enemy avoid whenever possible
- Write typescript types Matt Pocock would be proud of

## Documentation First Development

When a project has a docs folder I like to first read the docs, then add or modify them to signal the changes I'm about to do.

I like my documentation to specify intent and, generally, the goal of the application and tools. I do not want rambling or unnecessary embellishments or explanations. Also, this is not spec-driven docs; any mentions of code in docs should be links to files in the code. Things like colors or border sizes, etc., aren't needed in docs unless that is what the project is all about.

My documentation is always written with the intent to track what the goals were and to help track drift in requirements during code reviews.

- Search with `rg`/`fd`, not `grep -r`/`find`, take advantage of the tools on the machine

Default to researching questions online rather than relying solely on training data, especially for:
- Claims that need verification
- Topics where recent developments matter
- Questions where multiple credible sources would strengthen the answer
- Anything involving current events, statistics, or facts that could be outdated

Be a constructive skeptic: Ask probing questions, suggest alternative perspectives, and highlight potential counterarguments. If you disagree with something I've said, explain why clearly.

Stay collegial but not deferential. Treat this as a collaboration between equals working through problems together. Avoid:
- Excessive positivity or cheerleading
- Defaulting to "that's a great idea" without substantive analysis
- Hedging every critique with compliments
- Assuming I'm right just because I stated something confidently

Be direct. If something seems unclear, ask probing questions.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

# Benchmark Data

A fixed snapshot of NASA/JPL small-body and planetary data. **Read-only** — do
not modify, move, or delete anything in this directory. Load it at runtime with
`fetch` (relative paths); make no external network calls.

Provenance and exact query URLs are in [`provenance.json`](./provenance.json).
The snapshot is regenerated by `scripts/fetch-data.mjs` + `scripts/build-planets.mjs`.

## Files

| file | what | rows |
|---|---|---|
| `asteroids.json` | All known Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) with orbital + physical data | ~42,000 |
| `close-approaches.json` | NEO close-approach events to Earth | ~50,000 |
| `planets.json` | The eight planets' orbital elements + radii | 8 |
| `comets.json` | Comets, same element schema (optional overlay) | ~4,000 |
| `sentry.json` | CNEOS impact-risk summary (optional overlay) | ~2,200 |
| `provenance.json` | Sources, query URLs, retrieval timestamp | — |

All three data files are **arrays of objects**. Values are numbers or `null`
(many physical fields are unknown for less-studied objects).

## Coordinate & element conventions

Orbital elements describe a heliocentric orbit in the **J2000 ecliptic** frame.
Angles are in **degrees**, distances in **astronomical units (au)**, time in
**days**. Each object carries its **own** `epoch` (a Julian date) — propagate
each body from its own epoch.

Positions are **not** stored; they must be **computed** from the elements for a
chosen time (i.e. solve the orbit / Kepler's equation and advance the mean
anomaly by the mean motion). The Sun is the central body, at the origin, with a
mean radius of **696,000 km**.

### Orbital element fields (in `asteroids.json` and `planets.json`)

| field | meaning | unit |
|---|---|---|
| `a` | semi-major axis | au |
| `e` | eccentricity | — |
| `i` | inclination | deg |
| `om` | longitude of ascending node (Ω) | deg |
| `w` | argument of perihelion (ω) | deg |
| `ma` | mean anomaly at epoch | deg |
| `epoch` | epoch of the elements | Julian date |
| `n` | mean motion (deg/day) — present on planets; derivable elsewhere | deg/day |
| `per` | orbital period | days |
| `q`, `ad` | perihelion / aphelion distance | au |
| `tp` | time of perihelion passage | Julian date |

### `asteroids.json` — additional fields

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `full_name`, `pdes`, `name` | display name, primary designation, IAU name (may be null) |
| `spkid` | unique JPL SPK-ID |
| `neo`, `pha` | booleans: Near-Earth Object / Potentially Hazardous Asteroid |
| `class` | orbit class code (e.g. `APO`, `ATE`, `AMO`, `IEO`) |
| `moid` | minimum orbit intersection distance with Earth (au) |
| `H` | absolute magnitude (brightness) |
| `G` | magnitude slope parameter |
| `diameter` | estimated diameter (km) — often null |
| `albedo` | geometric albedo — often null |
| `rot_per` | rotation period (hours) — often null |
| `spec_B`, `spec_T` | spectral type (SMASSII / Tholen) — often null |
| `first_obs` | date of first observation |

### `planets.json` — additional fields

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | planet name |
| `radius_km` | mean radius (km) |

### `comets.json` (optional overlay)

Comets, using the **same orbital-element fields** as asteroids (`a e i om w ma
epoch q per n tp`) plus `full_name`, `pdes`, `class`, `M1` (total magnitude), and
`diameter`. **Caution:** roughly half are hyperbolic or near-parabolic
(`e >= 1`) — these have no period/mean-motion and must be propagated from `tp`
(time of perihelion passage), not from `ma`/`n`.

### `sentry.json` (optional overlay)

CNEOS Sentry impact-risk summary, one row per monitored object. Join to asteroids
on `des` ↔ asteroid `pdes`.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `des`, `fullname` | designation / display name |
| `ip` | cumulative impact probability |
| `ps_cum`, `ps_max` | cumulative / max Palermo scale |
| `ts_max` | max Torino scale (0–10) |
| `range` | year range of potential impacts |
| `n_imp` | number of potential impacts |
| `diameter`, `h`, `v_inf` | size (km), abs. magnitude, encounter velocity (km/s) |
| `last_obs`, `last_obs_jd` | last observation date |

### `close-approaches.json`

One row per Earth close-approach event. Join to asteroids on
`des` ↔ asteroid `pdes`.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `des` | object designation (matches asteroid `pdes`) |
| `cd` | close-approach date/time (calendar, TDB) |
| `jd` | close-approach time (Julian date) |
| `dist` | nominal approach distance (au) |
| `dist_min`, `dist_max` | 3σ distance bounds (au) |
| `v_rel`, `v_inf` | relative / unperturbed velocity (km/s) |
| `h` | absolute magnitude of the object |

# Benchmark Data

A fixed snapshot of NASA/JPL small-body and planetary data. **Read-only** — do
not modify, move, or delete anything in this directory. Load it at runtime with
`fetch` (relative paths); make no external network calls.

Provenance and exact query URLs are in [`provenance.json`](./provenance.json).
The snapshot is regenerated by `scripts/fetch-data.mjs` + `scripts/build-planets.mjs`.

## Files

| file | what | rows |
|---|---|---|
| `asteroids.json` | All known Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) with orbital + physical data | ~42,000 |
| `close-approaches.json` | NEO close-approach events to Earth | ~50,000 |
| `planets.json` | The eight planets' orbital elements + radii | 8 |
| `comets.json` | Comets, same element schema (optional overlay) | ~4,000 |
| `sentry.json` | CNEOS impact-risk summary (optional overlay) | ~2,200 |
| `provenance.json` | Sources, query URLs, retrieval timestamp | — |

All three data files are **arrays of objects**. Values are numbers or `null`
(many physical fields are unknown for less-studied objects).

## Coordinate & element conventions

Orbital elements describe a heliocentric orbit in the **J2000 ecliptic** frame.
Angles are in **degrees**, distances in **astronomical units (au)**, time in
**days**. Each object carries its **own** `epoch` (a Julian date) — propagate
each body from its own epoch.

Positions are **not** stored; they must be **computed** from the elements for a
chosen time (i.e. solve the orbit / Kepler's equation and advance the mean
anomaly by the mean motion). The Sun is the central body, at the origin, with a
mean radius of **696,000 km**.

### Orbital element fields (in `asteroids.json` and `planets.json`)

| field | meaning | unit |
|---|---|---|
| `a` | semi-major axis | au |
| `e` | eccentricity | — |
| `i` | inclination | deg |
| `om` | longitude of ascending node (Ω) | deg |
| `w` | argument of perihelion (ω) | deg |
| `ma` | mean anomaly at epoch | deg |
| `epoch` | epoch of the elements | Julian date |
| `n` | mean motion (deg/day) — present on planets; derivable elsewhere | deg/day |
| `per` | orbital period | days |
| `q`, `ad` | perihelion / aphelion distance | au |
| `tp` | time of perihelion passage | Julian date |

### `asteroids.json` — additional fields

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `full_name`, `pdes`, `name` | display name, primary designation, IAU name (may be null) |
| `spkid` | unique JPL SPK-ID |
| `neo`, `pha` | booleans: Near-Earth Object / Potentially Hazardous Asteroid |
| `class` | orbit class code (e.g. `APO`, `ATE`, `AMO`, `IEO`) |
| `moid` | minimum orbit intersection distance with Earth (au) |
| `H` | absolute magnitude (brightness) |
| `G` | magnitude slope parameter |
| `diameter` | estimated diameter (km) — often null |
| `albedo` | geometric albedo — often null |
| `rot_per` | rotation period (hours) — often null |
| `spec_B`, `spec_T` | spectral type (SMASSII / Tholen) — often null |
| `first_obs` | date of first observation |

### `planets.json` — additional fields

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | planet name |
| `radius_km` | mean radius (km) |

### `comets.json` (optional overlay)

Comets, using the **same orbital-element fields** as asteroids (`a e i om w ma
epoch q per n tp`) plus `full_name`, `pdes`, `class`, `M1` (total magnitude), and
`diameter`. **Caution:** roughly half are hyperbolic or near-parabolic
(`e >= 1`) — these have no period/mean-motion and must be propagated from `tp`
(time of perihelion passage), not from `ma`/`n`.

### `sentry.json` (optional overlay)

CNEOS Sentry impact-risk summary, one row per monitored object. Join to asteroids
on `des` ↔ asteroid `pdes`.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `des`, `fullname` | designation / display name |
| `ip` | cumulative impact probability |
| `ps_cum`, `ps_max` | cumulative / max Palermo scale |
| `ts_max` | max Torino scale (0–10) |
| `range` | year range of potential impacts |
| `n_imp` | number of potential impacts |
| `diameter`, `h`, `v_inf` | size (km), abs. magnitude, encounter velocity (km/s) |
| `last_obs`, `last_obs_jd` | last observation date |

### `close-approaches.json`

One row per Earth close-approach event. Join to asteroids on
`des` ↔ asteroid `pdes`.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `des` | object designation (matches asteroid `pdes`) |
| `cd` | close-approach date/time (calendar, TDB) |
| `jd` | close-approach time (Julian date) |
| `dist` | nominal approach distance (au) |
| `dist_min`, `dist_max` | 3σ distance bounds (au) |
| `v_rel`, `v_inf` | relative / unperturbed velocity (km/s) |
| `h` | absolute magnitude of the object |

# NEO Orrery

An interactive 3D orrery of the inner solar system and its ~42,000 near-Earth asteroids,
built from the JPL snapshot in [`data/`](data/README.md). See [`PLAN.md`](PLAN.md) for the brief.

```sh
pnpm install && pnpm build   # static site in dist/
pnpm dev                     # local dev server
```

## Intent

A tool for exploring where near-Earth objects are, how they move, and which ones matter:

- **Every position is computed**, never stored: each body is propagated from its own epoch with
  two-body Kepler motion ([`src/orbit.ts`](src/orbit.ts)). Closed orbits use Kepler's equation,
  hyperbolic comets the hyperbolic form, and parabolic comets Barker's equation from perihelion time.
- **Time is the main control**: play/rewind at several speeds, scrub 1900–2200, jump to a date or
  to any recorded close approach.
- **Highlight what matters**: colour by hazard, orbit class, size, Earth MOID or Sentry Palermo
  scale ([`src/encoding.ts`](src/encoding.ts)); filter by hazard, class, size, MOID and close
  approaches near the current date; ranked lists of upcoming approaches, highest impact risk,
  closest recorded approaches and largest PHAs ([`src/panels.ts`](src/panels.ts)).
- **Investigate one object**: orbit, physical data with a size comparison, Sentry risk, live
  distance to Earth/Sun, and its close-approach history (clickable, also marked on the timeline).
- **Focus & follow** a body as time runs ([`src/scene.ts`](src/scene.ts)).
- **Shareable**: time, selection, follow, camera, colour mode and hazard filter live in the URL hash
  ([`src/url.ts`](src/url.ts)); "Copy link" copies it.

## Data pipeline

`pnpm build` runs [`scripts/prepare-data.ts`](scripts/prepare-data.ts), which reads `data/`
(never modified) and writes compact column-oriented JSON to `public/data/` → `dist/data/`.
It joins Sentry and close-approach rows to asteroids by designation and orders asteroids so
hazardous objects draw on top. The app fetches these files with relative URLs at runtime.

## Assumptions & limitations

- **Two-body only.** No planetary perturbations, so positions drift from reality the further
  you are from an object's epoch (decades → noticeable; Apophis in April 2029 lands a few LD
  off instead of 0.1 LD). The close-approach tables come from JPL's full integration and are the
  authoritative numbers; the "From Earth" live distance is the model's.
- Planets use mean J2000 elements without secular rates.
- Times are shown as UTC; the ~1 minute TDB–UTC difference is ignored.
- Diameters without a measurement are estimated from H assuming albedo 0.14 (marked "~").
- The Sun and planets are drawn as fixed-size glows so they stay visible; true-scale spheres
  appear when zoomed in close. Background stars are decorative, not a real catalogue.
- Comets are off by default; "periodic only" hides open (e ≥ 1) orbits, which are mostly far
  away at any given date.
EOF

content.text:
I've built the NEO Orrery: an interactive 3D view of the Sun, planets and all 42,075 near-Earth asteroids, plus every direction in the plan. A clean `pnpm install && pnpm build` succeeds and outputs a self-contained static site in `dist/` with relative URLs. `data/` is untouched. Assumptions and limitations are written down in `README.md`.

I checked it in headless Chrome. It runs at 60fps with all 42k objects moving, and it makes no external requests. The only `http` strings left in the bundle are an XML namespace and a comment inside three.js.

**How it works**
- **Positions:** each body's position is computed from its own epoch with two-body Kepler motion (`src/orbit.ts`). Closed orbits use Kepler's equation, hyperbolic comets the hyperbolic form, and parabolic comets Barker's equation from perihelion time. As a check, Earth comes out at 179.6° ecliptic longitude at the 2026 March equinox; it should be about 180°.
- **Data step:** `scripts/prepare-data.ts` runs during the build. It turns `data/` into compact JSON in `dist/data/` (16 MB of asteroids becomes 6 MB) and links the impact-risk and close-approach rows to their asteroids. The app loads these files with `fetch` at runtime.
- **Stack:** Vite, TypeScript and three.js, no UI framework. The 42k objects are drawn as one point cloud, and hidden objects aren't computed.

**Features**
- **Time:** play, reverse, speeds from 1 hour/s to 10 years/s, a 1900–2200 scrubber, a date picker and a Today button.
- **Colour by:** hazard, orbit class, size, closest distance to Earth's orbit (MOID), or Palermo impact-risk scale, each with a legend.
- **Filters:** hazard status, orbit class, minimum diameter, maximum MOID, and "has a close approach within ±N days of the current date".
- **Search** across asteroids, comets and planets.
- **Highlights tab:** next Earth close approaches (clicking one jumps there and frames Earth), highest impact risk, closest recorded approaches, and largest potentially hazardous asteroids.
- **Detail panel:**
  - live distance to the Sun and Earth, and speed
  - orbit and physical data, with a size comparison ("about the size of the Eiffel Tower")
  - impact-risk figures
  - a clickable close-approach table, with the same dates marked on the timeline
- **Comets:** a layer you can switch on. It shows periodic comets only, or all of them including open orbits.
- **Follow mode, deep links and context:** the camera can lock onto a body as time runs. Time, selection, follow, camera and colour mode are kept in the URL, with a Copy link button. Distance rings, a scale bar that switches between au, km and lunar distances (LD), and orbit lines for up to 1,500 shown asteroids help with scale.

**Limitations**
- **Positions drift from reality decades from the data's date.** The two-body model ignores pull from the planets. For Apophis on 13 April 2029 the model shows 2.5 LD, against the real 0.1 LD. The close-approach tables come from JPL's full calculation and are the numbers to trust. The detail panel shows both and the help text explains the difference.
- **Diameters are often estimated.** Most asteroids have no measured diameter, so size is estimated from brightness assuming an albedo of 0.14. Estimated values are marked with "~".

The tight cluster of comets you'll see when comets are on is real data: 78 fragments of comet 73P/Schwassmann–Wachmann on nearly the same orbit.

There's no `docs/` folder, so the intent and assumptions are in `README.md`, with links into the code.
